# Regulatory control map

This is a map from regulatory and standards provisions to what a2a-rust, a protocol library, provides toward them. It is not a claim that the SDK is compliant with anything: the EU AI Act places no obligation on this SDK, which is neither an AI system nor a provider (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 3(1) and 3(3)). Article 25(4) requires a written agreement between a high-risk system's provider and a third party supplying it components, and exempts from that agreement a third party making components other than general-purpose AI models accessible to the public under a free and open-source licence, as this SDK is; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 rewrote the paragraph's first subparagraph and kept the exemption. The exemption is from that paragraph only, not from the rest of Article 25. The obligations below belong to whoever builds an AI system or a product with this SDK. Each row says how much of one this SDK carries for them, with the test that proves it, and what is left. Not legal advice.

As of 2026-10-23. Every cited test is checked to exist, as a test, by `scripts/check_compliance_map.py` in CI; a row cannot outlive its evidence.

## EU AI Act — Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744

Source: <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng> — read in the primary text.

Article text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 read on EUR-Lex on 2026-10-08; the amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 read in its Official Journal edition (OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026; in force 27 July 2026) on 2026-10-15, every page rendered. Application dates, Article 113 as amended: Chapters I and II from 2 February 2025, except the Article 5 prohibitions 2026/1744 added, from 2 December 2026; Article 50 from 2 August 2026, with until 2 December 2026 for Article 50(2) where a generative system was on the market before 2 August 2026 (Article 111(4)); Annex III high-risk obligations from 2 December 2027; Annex I high-risk obligations from 2 August 2028. Annex XIV, added by 2026/1744, lists the types of AI system a notified body is designated to assess, and its code AIH 0401 names "Agentic AI": a high-risk system built from A2A agents has a category for its third-party conformity assessment. Articles 5, 6, 16, 43 and 47-49 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 read in its Official Journal edition (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024), fetched from the Publications Office on 2026-10-15, those pages rendered.

## Cyber Resilience Act — Regulation (EU) 2024/2847

Source: <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2847/oj/eng> — read in the primary text.

Article text read in the Official Journal edition (OJ L, 2024/2847, 20.11.2024) on 2026-10-21, fetched from the Publications Office (EUR-Lex answered with a challenge page). Application, Article 71(2): Article 14 from 11 September 2026, also for products placed on the market before 11 December 2027 (Article 69(3)); Chapter IV (Articles 35-51) from 11 June 2026; the rest from 11 December 2027. The Act applies to products made available on the market, that is supplied in the course of a commercial activity (Articles 2(1), 3(22)); free and open-source software that its manufacturer does not monetise is not (Recital 18), and an open-source software steward is a legal person (Article 3(14)), which this project's individual maintainer is not (CRA-24). These rows serve the manufacturers who integrate the crates, who must exercise due diligence on them (Article 13(5)).

## GDPR — Regulation (EU) 2016/679

Source: <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng> — read in the primary text.

Article text read in the Official Journal edition (OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1) on 2026-10-21, fetched from the Publications Office (EUR-Lex answered with a challenge page). The controller's and processor's obligations are theirs: the SDK is neither, and each row says what it offers toward one.

| ID | Provision | Requirement | What the SDK provides | Status | Evidence | Gap or reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GDPR-25-1 | Art. 25(1), 5(1)(c) | Data protection by design: measures such as pseudonymisation, implementing data minimisation. | Minimisation: audit records hold content only as digests; message content is kept out of spans unless the operator opts in; `CallContext` debug output names headers but never prints their values; the JWT validator, push configuration and token provider redact their secrets in debug output. Pseudonymisation, with the `encryption` feature: `AuditLog::with_privacy` seals each person an audit record names under a key of their own, records carry only a random handle, and each digest is an HMAC bound to its record that confirms no guess without the key (ADR 0015, amended 2026-10-16); `EncryptedTaskStore` seals every part of a task and of its event log; the SQL push-config stores seal each config. | Supported | `every_call_and_event_is_recorded_and_attributable`<br>`the_executor_span_is_invoke_agent_without_content_by_default`<br>`debug_prints_header_names_and_never_their_values`<br>`debug_impls_render_type_and_redact_secrets`<br>`debug_redacts_secrets_but_keeps_presence`<br>`debug_redacts_secrets`<br>`a_handler_over_the_wrapper_stores_no_plaintext_and_serves_it_whole`<br>`with_a_cipher_no_secret_is_stored_and_the_config_reads_back`<br>`a_served_call_is_recorded_naming_no_one_and_erasable`<br>`a_digest_is_checked_with_the_key_and_cannot_be_confirmed_without_it`<br>`one_content_in_two_records_carries_two_tags` | Left to the integrator: What the stores query (ids, states, timestamps, `metadata`) stays readable to them, so personal data belongs out of those fields; and the measures are the operator's to switch on (what is on by default is GDPR-25-2). |

| GDPR-32-1d | Art. 32(1)(d) | A process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of the processing. | The SDK's own measures are tested on every pull request and on a schedule: fuzz targets over the parsers and over every reader of sealed values at rest, nightly; mutation testing, incremental on pull requests and a full sweep weekly; the sealed formats decrypted by an independent implementation, and AES-256-GCM checked against NIST test vectors; CodeQL and OSV-Scanner; and this map's citations checked to exist. | Integrator's duty | `nist_decrypt_cases_open_or_are_refused_as_nist_says`<br>CI: cargo +nightly fuzz run<br>CI: cargo mutants -p ${{ matrix.crate }}<br>CI: scripts/crypto_interop/check.py<br>CI: github/codeql-action/analyze<br>CI: google/osv-scanner-action/.github/workflows/osv-scanner-reusable-pr.yml<br>CI: scripts/check_compliance_map.py --check<br>[security-testing.md](../../book/src/deployment/security-testing.md) | The process the article asks for tests the measures of a processing operation: its configuration, keys, access control and infrastructure, which are the controller's and processor's. The SDK's CI covers the library's code only, not how a deployment uses it. |
| GDPR-33-34 | Art. 33, 34 | A personal data breach (a breach of security leading to the destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data, Art. 4(12)) is notified to the supervisory authority without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours, and documented; a processor notifies the controller; where the breach is likely to result in a high risk, it is communicated to the data subjects, unless, among other conditions, the data were rendered unintelligible to unauthorised persons, such as by encryption (Art. 34(3)(a)). | Evidence for detecting and documenting one: the audit chain, verified with `log.verify` or offline with `a2a audit verify`, names the first record edited, deleted or reordered, and a tail cut past a signed checkpoint; refused calls are recorded with their outcome. Toward Art. 34(3)(a), `EncryptedTaskStore` and `AuditLog::with_privacy` leave content and the people records name unintelligible without the keys (GDPR-32-1a). | Integrator's duty | `a_resealed_edit_breaks_the_next_link`<br>`a_deleted_record_is_a_gap`<br>`truncating_the_tail_past_a_checkpoint_is_found`<br>`an_exported_chain_verifies_and_an_edited_one_names_where_it_breaks`<br>`every_call_and_event_is_recorded_and_attributable` | Detecting a breach, assessing its risk, and notifying the authority and the people concerned are the controller's acts, and a processor's notice to the controller is the processor's. The SDK verifies a chain only when asked and raises no alert. Encryption leaves ids, states, timestamps and `metadata` readable, so whether a breach of an encrypted store left the personal data unintelligible depends on what the integrator put in those fields. |
| GDPR-35 | Art. 35 | Where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller assesses the impact of the envisaged processing on the protection of personal data before processing; the assessment describes the processing and its purposes, assesses necessity, proportionality and risks, and states the measures envisaged to address them. | Inputs to the description of measures (35(7)(d)): this control map; the security chapter, which lists what encryption at rest does and does not protect and the SDK's known gaps; ADR 0015, which states what the audit trail records, the threats it answers and what erasure does not reach. AIA-26-27 notes that a fundamental rights impact assessment under the AI Act may draw on a DPIA. | Integrator's duty | CI: python3 scripts/check_compliance_map.py --check<br>[security.md](../../book/src/deployment/security.md)<br>[0015-audit-trail.md](../../docs/adr/0015-audit-trail.md) | The assessment concerns the controller's processing, purposes and risks to the people affected, and is carried out by the controller; a library can describe its own measures but not a deployment's necessity, proportionality or risk. |
| GDPR-44-49 | Art. 44–49 | A transfer of personal data to a third country or an international organisation, onward transfers included, takes place only under the conditions of Chapter V: an adequacy decision (Art. 45), appropriate safeguards with enforceable rights and remedies (Art. 46, 47), or a derogation for a specific situation (Art. 49). | Where personal data go is set by configuration: the agents the client is told to call, the webhook URLs callers register, which `HttpPushSender::with_allowed_hosts` limits to listed hosts, and the telemetry exporter's endpoint. The SDK records no destination's location. | Integrator's duty | code: `HttpPushSender::with_allowed_hosts`<br>`the_host_allowlist_refuses_other_hosts_before_connecting` | Whether a destination is in a third country, and the legal ground for sending data there, are the controller's and processor's to establish; a host name says nothing about where data are processed. Peer agents and webhook receivers may transfer onward. |

## OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)

Source: <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/> — **identifiers and wording from secondary sources; check against the published text before relying on them**.

Published 9 December 2025. The identifiers and names below agree across three secondary summaries; OWASP's own page carries the list only as a download.

| ID | Provision | Requirement | What the SDK provides | Status | Evidence | Gap or reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ASI03 | ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse | Agents act under identities and delegated privileges that are scoped, attributable and not escalated. | Authenticated callers are named, and the name reaches the executor through the request context. A delegated call carries the originating principal as an RFC 8693 token whose `act` chain names the agents acting for it (`TokenExchange` on the client; `CallContext::actors` and the audit record on the server, ADR 0021); the identity provider scopes what may be delegated. | Partial | `a_labelled_api_key_names_its_caller`<br>`an_executor_sees_the_caller_identity_the_interceptor_established`<br>`every_call_and_event_is_recorded_and_attributable`<br>`a_delegated_token_names_its_principal_and_its_actors`<br>`a_record_names_the_agents_that_acted_for_its_caller`<br>`an_exchange_sends_rfc_8693_parameters_and_reads_the_issued_token` | The originating principal travels only where the identity provider supports RFC 8693 token exchange and the delegating agent uses it; otherwise a delegated call carries the delegating agent's credential, and the chain is joined afterwards through the trace id. Scope attenuation is the identity provider's policy. |
| ASI04 | ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities | Agents, tools and schemas an agent imports are verified before they are trusted. | Agent cards can be signed (JWS over RFC 8785 canonical form, ES256 or EdDSA) and verified against a raw or SPKI key, or against a JWK Set by `kid`, trying every signature the card carries (key rotation). The client fetches a JWK Set from a URL the caller trusts, over HTTPS, bounded in size and time; removing a key from the set revokes it, and a key whose `exp` has passed, or whose `x5c` leaf certificate is outside its validity period or holds another key, is never used (spec §8.4.3, RFC 7517 §4.7). | Partial | `sign_and_verify_agent_card`<br>`verify_rejects_tampered_card`<br>`a_jwks_verifies_by_kid_and_alg`<br>`removing_a_key_from_the_set_revokes_it`<br>`an_expired_key_is_not_used`<br>`the_rfc_8037_ed25519_example_verifies`<br>`a_card_verifies_under_a_fetched_set`<br>`x5c_expired_leaf_is_not_used`<br>`x5c_leaf_holding_another_key_is_not_used`<br>`a_fetched_key_whose_certificate_has_expired_is_not_used` | Not built: validating an `x5c` chain to a trust anchor, its certificates' signatures, and CRL/OCSP revocation. Which key set to trust is the caller's decision: the SDK never follows a `jku` taken from the card itself. A key's expiry is honoured from `exp` (which RFC 7517 does not define) and from its `x5c` leaf's validity period. Tools and schemas an agent imports outside A2A are out of scope. |
| ASI07 | ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication | Messages between agents are authenticated and protected against interception and forgery. | TLS on every client transport and on the server's HTTP, WebSocket and gRPC listeners, mutual TLS on each with the client certificate naming the caller (MutualTlsAuthInterceptor), authenticated calls, signed agent cards, and signed messages and artifacts (the provenance extension) that a receiver can verify end to end, across intermediaries. | Partial | `tls_client_rejects_unknown_ca`<br>`a_signed_message_verifies_under_either_algorithm`<br>`a_listener_requiring_client_certificates_serves_only_clients_with_one`<br>`the_client_certificate_names_the_caller_over_https`<br>`the_client_certificate_names_the_caller_over_wss`<br>`the_client_certificate_names_the_caller_over_grpc` | Signing messages and artifacts (the provenance extension) is opt-in, and verifying them is the receiver's call; unsigned content can still be altered by an intermediary that terminates TLS. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy the listener sees no client certificate, so mutual TLS names the caller only on a listener that terminates TLS itself (ADR 0018). |
| ASI08 | ASI08 Cascading Failures | A failure in one agent or tool does not propagate unchecked through the agents that depend on it. | Per-caller rate limits, per-tenant concurrency limits, an executor timeout, bounded queues and stores. A `Delegation` cancels a task's children on other agents when the task is cancelled, its stream to a child is lost, or its handle is dropped; with a lease (`Delegation::start_leased`, ADR 0020) a child whose parent crashes or goes quiet is stopped by its own server. A budget (ADR 0023) carries the parent's deadline and named meters to the child: every server holds a turn to the caller's deadline, and `BudgetHandle::grant` reserves each meter from the parent and refunds only on the settling report, so a child's deadline sits inside its parent's (timed from receipt) and a meter cannot be granted twice over. | Partial | `fast_path_rate_limit_exceeded`<br>`a_tenant_at_its_concurrency_limit_is_refused`<br>`a_lost_stream_cancels_the_child`<br>`dropping_an_unsettled_handle_cancels_the_child`<br>`a_child_whose_parent_goes_quiet_stops`<br>`a_live_parent_keeps_its_child_running`<br>`a_grandchilds_deadline_is_inside_its_parents`<br>`the_parent_is_charged_what_the_child_spent`<br>`the_callers_deadline_ends_the_turn_before_the_servers_timeout`<br>`ten_children_cannot_each_be_given_the_whole` | Leases are opt-in on both sides: a child on an agent that grants none, or sent without one, runs on after its parent crashes. A peer that does not implement the budget extension ignores the budget, a meter's unit means only what the agents agree, and a child that under-reports its spend is refunded more than it should be. |
| ASI09 | ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation | Sensitive actions require explicit human confirmation rather than trust in confident output. | The approval extension binds a person's confirmation to the digest of the exact action, and the `ApprovalGate` refuses a confirmation of anything else, from anyone not allowed, or from the caller who asked; each admitted confirmation is an audit record. | Supported | code: `ApprovalGate`<br>code: `EventEmitter::request_approval`<br>`an_approval_flows_through_the_gate_to_the_executor`<br>`a_decision_for_another_request_or_action_is_refused`<br>`who_may_approve`<br>`without_a_gate_a_decision_is_never_reported_as_checked`<br>`an_admitted_decision_is_audited_with_the_approver` | Left to the integrator: Which actions are sensitive enough to ask about is the executor's decision; the SDK cannot make it ask (re-examined 2026-10-20: the confirmation path is built and tested end to end). |
| ASI10 | ASI10 Rogue Agents | Agents acting outside their intended behaviour are detected and stopped. | Spans and metrics for every call; cancellation of a task; `RequestHandler::halt`, which stops every task of a tenant or of the server and refuses new ones until resumed, on every replica sharing a halt store and across restarts (ADR 0019), pushed with the write by the PostgreSQL and in-memory stores (ADR 0024); a cancel is pushed to the replica running the task. | Partial | `cancel_task_signals_cancellation_token`<br>`halting_all_cancels_every_tenant`<br>`a_halt_on_one_replica_stops_and_refuses_on_the_other`<br>`a_halt_is_pushed_to_the_other_replica`<br>`a_cancel_is_pushed_to_the_replica_running_the_task`<br>`the_in_memory_halt_store_conforms`<br>`the_sqlite_halt_store_conforms`<br>`each_flaw_is_named` | Nothing detects a rogue agent: deciding to halt is a person's or an integrator's monitor's. A halt reaches other replicas only through a halt store; one that does not push (SQLite, a custom store) is followed within its poll interval. A custom store is graded by `conformance::halt`. A pushed cancel fires the running executor's token, and an executor that ignores its token runs on. |
| ASI-MODEL | ASI01, ASI02, ASI05, ASI06 | Goal hijack, tool misuse, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning. | A client interceptor sees each request's params and each response's result, so an integrator's content filter or policy on what an agent sends and receives runs there; a server interceptor sees only the call context (method, caller, tenant, headers) and can refuse a call from it, and the message reaches only the executor, where a filter on what an agent is sent runs. When the model is hijacked anyway, the SDK contains the effects: a repeated side-effecting tool call runs once, the turn bound and the caller's token budget end a runaway run, content whose signature fails is refused before the model reads it, an approval gate refuses the requester's own approval, delegated budgets bound what children spend, a halt stops the run, and caller isolation hides other callers' tasks. `docs/injection-containment.md` has each scenario, against a model that obeys every instruction it reads. | Integrator's duty | `a_repeated_payment_planted_in_a_page_runs_once`<br>`the_callers_token_budget_ends_the_run_sooner`<br>`an_impostors_answer_is_refused_before_the_model_reads_it`<br>`an_unsigned_answer_is_refused_when_signatures_are_required`<br>`an_agent_cannot_approve_the_action_it_requested`<br>`fan_out_stops_when_the_parents_budget_is_reserved`<br>`another_callers_task_cannot_be_read_on_an_injected_instruction`<br>`a_halt_stops_an_injected_run_and_refuses_new_work`<br>[injection-containment.md](../../docs/injection-containment.md) | Preventing the hijack is the integrator's: these attack the model, its tools and its memory, which live in the executor. What the SDK does not contain, each asserted by a test: differing side-effecting calls run until the turn bound or budget ends the run; unsigned content passes unless signatures are required; a trusted agent that is compromised is still obeyed, since a signature says who wrote content, not that it is safe. |

## ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — AI management systems

Source: <https://www.iso.org/standard/81230.html> — **identifiers and wording from secondary sources; check against the published text before relying on them**.

A management-system standard: an organisation is certified against it, a library is not. Annex A control numbers are taken from secondary sources, which disagree on some of them; check against the published standard.

| ID | Provision | Requirement | What the SDK provides | Status | Evidence | Gap or reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISO42001-A.6.2.8 | Annex A.6.2.8, AI system recording of event logs (numbering unverified) | The organisation determines at which life-cycle phases event logging is enabled, at minimum while the AI system is in use. | As for AIA-12-1: the audit trail, on whenever the handler is built with it. | Supported | `every_call_and_event_is_recorded_and_attributable` | — |
| ISO42001-AIMS | Clauses 4–10 | An AI management system: policy, roles, risk assessment, impact assessment, monitoring, improvement. | Nothing beyond the records above. | Integrator's duty | `every_call_and_event_is_recorded_and_attributable` | A management system is an organisation's; a library cannot hold one. |
